items.readable_text:
Content:
Interesting mathematical problems often involve a large (or infinite) collection of sets. Labeling each set with a subscript is often convenient in such situations.

Content:
For example, suppose we define a collection of sets [MATH: A_i] for [MATH: i\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A_1 = \{1,2\}, \qquad A_2 = \{3,4\}, \qquad A_3 = \{5,6\}, \qquad \ldots]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- This collection of [MATH: A_i]'s, which we denote [MATH: \big\{ A_i \big\}_{i \in \mathbb N},] is called a family of indexed sets.
- The set [MATH: i=\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N] is called the index set.

Content:
Writing each set with a subscript makes talking about a general [MATH: A_i] easier. In this particular case, for example, we can express a general member of this family in terms of its index:

Content:
[MATH: A_i = \{2i-1,\, 2i\}, \qquad i\in\mathbb N]

Content:
So, if we wanted to write down the elements of [MATH: A_{100},] we substitute [MATH: i=100] into the definition of [MATH: A_i{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A_{100} = \big\{2(100)-1,\, 2(100)\big\} = \{199,200\}]

Content:
We can use any index set when defining a family of indexed sets.

Content:
For example, consider the indexed family [MATH: \big\{ B_x \big\}_{x \in \mathbb R},] where [MATH: B_x] is the real interval defined by

Content:
[MATH: B_x = \big[ 0, x^2 \big), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
Here, the index set is [MATH: \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
To write down, say, the elements of [MATH: B_{\color{blue}\sqrt{5}},] we substitute [MATH: x={\color{blue}\sqrt{5}}] into our definition of [MATH: B_x{:}]

Content:
[MATH: B_{sqrt(5)}|= [0, (sqrt(5))^{2}); = [0, 5)]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we have the indexed family [MATH: \{A_i\}_{i\in I}] where [MATH: I] is an index set.

Content:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to at least one set in the indexed family:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for at least one } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}]
where [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following family of indexed sets:

Content:
[MATH: X_i = \{ -i, \,0, \, i \}, \qquad i\in \mathbb N]

Content:
We wish to calculate the following union:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i]

Content:
To calculate our union, let's write down a few of our indexed sets:

Content:
- If [MATH: i=1,] we have [MATH: X_1 = \{ -1, 0, 1 \}.]
- If [MATH: i=2,] we have [MATH: X_2 = \{ -2, 0, 2 \}.]
- If [MATH: i=3,] we have [MATH: X_3 = \{ -3, 0, 3 \}.]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on.

Content:
Now, note the following:

Content:
- It's clear that the [MATH: X_i]'s contain only integers. Therefore, any union of [MATH: X_i]'s will contain only integers. So,
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i \subseteq \mathbb Z.]
- Notice that any integer [MATH: n] belongs to our union. For instance, [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}] lies in [MATH: X_n=\{ -n, 0, n \}] and, consequently, lies in the union of all [MATH: X_i]'s. Therefore,
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i \supseteq \mathbb Z.]

Content:
Thus, using the fact that [MATH: A\subseteq B] and [MATH: B\subseteq A] if and only if [MATH: A=B,] we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: ⋃_(i ∈ N)X_{i}|= {− 1, 0, 1}^(⏞)^(X_{1})∪{− 2, 0, 2}^(⏞)^(X_{2})∪{− 3, 0, 3}^(⏞)^(X_{3})∪⋯ = Z]

Content:
Finally, since our index set [MATH: I = \mathbb N] in this example, we can also use the following notation:

Content:
[MATH: ⋃_(i = 1)^(∞)X_{i} = Z]

Content:
Similarly, the intersection of a family of indexed sets [MATH: \{A_i\}_{i\in I}] contains all elements that belong to all sets in our family:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for all } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}]
where [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following family of indexed sets:

Content:
[MATH: S_i = \left[ 0, \: 10^{-i} \right], \qquad i \in \mathbb{N}]

Content:
We wish to compute the following intersection:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcap_{i \in \mathbb{N}} S_i]

Content:
To calculate our intersection, let's write down a few of our indexed sets:

Content:
- If [MATH: i=1,] we have [MATH: S_1 = [0, 0.1]]
- If [MATH: i=2,] we have [MATH: S_2 = \left[ 0, 0.01 \right]]
- If [MATH: i=3,] we have [MATH: S_3 = \left[ 0, 0.001 \right]]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on.

Content:
Now, note the following:

Content:
- As [MATH: i] increases, the right endpoint of [MATH: S_i] approaches [MATH: 0] but never reaches it.
- The left endpoint equals zero for each [MATH: S_i.]

Content:
So, the only element that lies in all sets is [MATH: 0.] Therefore, the intersection of our indexed family is the set containing zero only:

Content:
[MATH: ⋂_(i ∈ N)S_{i} = {0}.]

Content:
Finally, since our index set [MATH: I = \mathbb N] in this example, we can also use the following notation:

Content:
[MATH: ⋂_(i = 1)^(∞)S_{i} = {0}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Interesting mathematical problems often involve a large (or infinite) collection of sets. Labeling each set with a subscript is often convenient in such situations.

Content:
For example, suppose we define a collection of sets [MATH: A_i] for [MATH: i\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A_1 = \{1,2\}, \qquad A_2 = \{3,4\}, \qquad A_3 = \{5,6\}, \qquad \ldots]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- This collection of [MATH: A_i]'s, which we denote [MATH: \big\{ A_i \big\}_{i \in \mathbb N},] is called a family of indexed sets.
- The set [MATH: i=\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N] is called the index set.

Content:
Writing each set with a subscript makes talking about a general [MATH: A_i] easier. In this particular case, for example, we can express a general member of this family in terms of its index:

Content:
[MATH: A_i = \{2i-1,\, 2i\}, \qquad i\in\mathbb N]

Content:
So, if we wanted to write down the elements of [MATH: A_{100},] we substitute [MATH: i=100] into the definition of [MATH: A_i{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A_{100} = \big\{2(100)-1,\, 2(100)\big\} = \{199,200\}]

Content:
We can use any index set when defining a family of indexed sets.

Content:
For example, consider the indexed family [MATH: \big\{ B_x \big\}_{x \in \mathbb R},] where [MATH: B_x] is the real interval defined by

Content:
[MATH: B_x = \big[ 0, x^2 \big), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
Here, the index set is [MATH: \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
To write down, say, the elements of [MATH: B_{\color{blue}\sqrt{5}},] we substitute [MATH: x={\color{blue}\sqrt{5}}] into our definition of [MATH: B_x{:}]

Content:
[MATH: B_{sqrt(5)}|= [0, (sqrt(5))^{2}); = [0, 5)]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Elements of an Indexed Family

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: T_2] given that [MATH: T_n = \{ 1, 2, \ldots, 2n+1 \},] where [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To write down the elements of [MATH: T_2,] we substitute [MATH: n=2] into the expression and get

[MATH: T_{2}|= {1, 2, …, 2(2) + 1}; = {1, 2, …, 5}; = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Unions of Indexed  Families

Content:
Suppose we have the indexed family [MATH: \{A_i\}_{i\in I}] where [MATH: I] is an index set.

Content:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to at least one set in the indexed family:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for at least one } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}]
where [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following family of indexed sets:

Content:
[MATH: X_i = \{ -i, \,0, \, i \}, \qquad i\in \mathbb N]

Content:
We wish to calculate the following union:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i]

Content:
To calculate our union, let's write down a few of our indexed sets:

Content:
- If [MATH: i=1,] we have [MATH: X_1 = \{ -1, 0, 1 \}.]
- If [MATH: i=2,] we have [MATH: X_2 = \{ -2, 0, 2 \}.]
- If [MATH: i=3,] we have [MATH: X_3 = \{ -3, 0, 3 \}.]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on.

Content:
Now, note the following:

Content:
- It's clear that the [MATH: X_i]'s contain only integers. Therefore, any union of [MATH: X_i]'s will contain only integers. So,
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i \subseteq \mathbb Z.]
- Notice that any integer [MATH: n] belongs to our union. For instance, [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}] lies in [MATH: X_n=\{ -n, 0, n \}] and, consequently, lies in the union of all [MATH: X_i]'s. Therefore,
[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i \supseteq \mathbb Z.]

Content:
Thus, using the fact that [MATH: A\subseteq B] and [MATH: B\subseteq A] if and only if [MATH: A=B,] we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: ⋃_(i ∈ N)X_{i}|= {− 1, 0, 1}^(⏞)^(X_{1})∪{− 2, 0, 2}^(⏞)^(X_{2})∪{− 3, 0, 3}^(⏞)^(X_{3})∪⋯ = Z]

Content:
Finally, since our index set [MATH: I = \mathbb N] in this example, we can also use the following notation:

Content:
[MATH: ⋃_(i = 1)^(∞)X_{i} = Z]

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: Intersections of Indexed  Families

Content:
Similarly, the intersection of a family of indexed sets [MATH: \{A_i\}_{i\in I}] contains all elements that belong to all sets in our family:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for all } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}]
where [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following family of indexed sets:

Content:
[MATH: S_i = \left[ 0, \: 10^{-i} \right], \qquad i \in \mathbb{N}]

Content:
We wish to compute the following intersection:

Content:
[MATH: \bigcap_{i \in \mathbb{N}} S_i]

Content:
To calculate our intersection, let's write down a few of our indexed sets:

Content:
- If [MATH: i=1,] we have [MATH: S_1 = [0, 0.1]]
- If [MATH: i=2,] we have [MATH: S_2 = \left[ 0, 0.01 \right]]
- If [MATH: i=3,] we have [MATH: S_3 = \left[ 0, 0.001 \right]]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on.

Content:
Now, note the following:

Content:
- As [MATH: i] increases, the right endpoint of [MATH: S_i] approaches [MATH: 0] but never reaches it.
- The left endpoint equals zero for each [MATH: S_i.]

Content:
So, the only element that lies in all sets is [MATH: 0.] Therefore, the intersection of our indexed family is the set containing zero only:

Content:
[MATH: ⋂_(i ∈ N)S_{i} = {0}.]

Content:
Finally, since our index set [MATH: I = \mathbb N] in this example, we can also use the following notation:

Content:
[MATH: ⋂_(i = 1)^(∞)S_{i} = {0}]

---

Item 8 — Example: Finding Unions and Intersections of Finite Families of Indexed Sets

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \,\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} S_i], given that [MATH: I = \{ -1, 0, 1 \},] and [MATH: S_i = (i-1, \,i+1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to at least one set in the indexed family:

[MATH: \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for at least one } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}]
where [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Therefore, in our case, we have

[MATH: ⋃_(i ∈ I)S_{i}|= S_{− 1}∪S_{0}∪S_{1}; = (− 2, 0)∪(− 1, 1)∪(0, 2); = (− 2, 2).]

---
